name: Laban and the changed wages
charge: Changing his hired servant's wages ten times, and giving the elder daughter in place of the younger
summary: He took seven years' work for Rachel and delivered Leah, then charged another seven. He changed the wages ten times over twenty years. When Jacob left, he pursued him seven days with his brethren, and God came to him in a dream by night and told him to speak neither good nor bad. He searched the tents for his gods, found nothing, and went home having made a covenant at the heap.
offense: Two statutes are engaged. The substitution of Leah was fraud in a contract already performed, and his justification, that it must not be so done in our country to give the younger before the firstborn (Genesis 29:26), is a rule he had known before he took the seven years (Genesis 29:18). The changed wages are the graver charge because they were continuous (Genesis 31:7): Jacob's account, which Laban does not deny, is that thou hast changed my wages ten times (Genesis 31:41), and that but for the God of his father he would have been sent away empty (Genesis 31:42). Deuteronomy 24 forbids oppressing a hired servant that is poor and needy (Deuteronomy 24:14) and requires his wages the same day (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). Laban himself acknowledged that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob's sake, and Jacob recalled how little Laban had before his arrival (Genesis 30:27-30). He recognized the benefit of Jacob's service, yet continued changing the terms. The second seven years did not mean that Jacob waited fourteen years to receive Rachel. After completing Leah's week, he received Rachel also and served the further seven years (Genesis 29:27-30). The wrong lay in changing the agreement after the first service was performed. Jacob's later testimony joins the two periods of marriage service to six years for the cattle, amid heat, frost, sleeplessness, and repeated changes of wages (Genesis 31:38-41).
judgment: The pursuer was restrained before he could carry out his power to harm. God came to him in a dream and restrained him (Genesis 31:24), take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad (Genesis 31:24), and he admits it to Jacob's face, that it is in the power of my hand to do you hurt (Genesis 31:29), but the God of your father spake unto me yesternight. He made a covenant witnessed by a heap and a pillar, agreeing not to pass that boundary to harm Jacob (Genesis 31:46-52). God had seen Jacob's affliction and the labour of his hands, and rebuked Laban (Genesis 31:42). The record does not reduce Laban to poverty or give an accounting of repaid wages; it shows his power checked and Jacob departing with the household and substance God had preserved.
